units.translation: You must look upon this matter calmly and with self-control, and not neglect these gods.
Why must I tell you the name?
Where one must dwell in houses.
And indeed one must bring water for washing the feet of the god-bearers.
Before such words one must bite one's tongue.
The truly fortunate man must stay at home.
When must the end of these toils be accomplished?
When must you, having reached the end of these labors, see it?
But if one must obtain safety.
From these, your son Orestes is not standing by you here, as he should.
Should you not have driven this man out of this land? (thus Porson for χρή)
It was necessary that we did these things.
Since you love this man, but hate the one you should love.
You killed whom you should not have, and suffer what is not fated.

To the verb χρήζω [to need] is to be referred the participle κεχρημένος [needing], as χρῆς [you need] and χρῇ [he needs] are said for χρήζεις [you need] and χρήζει [he needs], on which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1649. Hesychius explained it by ἐνδεής ὢν [being in need] and χρήζων [needing]. It is read more often in Homer, either used absolutely or constructed with the genitive.
where κρυπτά [hidden things], read after χρήζων [needing], Hermann deleted, because it is a gloss on the word ἀλαά [blind things]. These are rather improbable conjectures.

Aeschylus constructed it with the infinitive. For thus what is read in M as κεχρημένοι [needing] seems to have been correctly corrected from the later scholium, which explains it as χρείαν ἔχοντα καὶ ἄξιον ὄντα σωφρονεῖν [having need and being worthy to be prudent], as Thomas Magister also interpreted κεχρημένος [needing] by χρήζοντες [needing], and similarly Hermann: you, whose interest it is that he be wise, admonish him. Others compared σωφρονεϊν κεχρημένον [needing to be prudent] with σωφρονεῖν εἰρημένον [said to be prudent] at Ag. 1620, so that the oracles mentioned above at 739 and 801 are referred to.
You do not need me as a teacher.
Having destroyed the whole race, he desired to plant another new one.
For I would not have desired to see these things.
I desire to hear your labors throughout.
For you first desired to learn of this.
For a god desiring to unite with this mortal woman.
You indeed speak these things which you desire, tongue of Zeus.
You seem to say nothing of what your father desires.
But still, desiring from these things, Zeus might make sounds more melodious.
And many other things he will reveal (the blind things he will reveal, as Hermann to satisfy the meter), desiring,
Therefore admonish him, who needs to be prudent, with reasonable warnings.
having need and being worthy to be prudent

hence Pr. 298 ἔα, τί χρῆμα; [ah, what is this?] perhaps τί χρῆμα λεύσσω [what do I see?] should be written, with ἔα [ah] placed outside the verse, as in Ch. 10 ἔα [ah] seems to be added before τί χρήμα λεύσσω [what do I see?].
